newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Firing erupts as rebels close in on Zaire city.
newsitem.headline: Firing erupts as rebels close in on Zaire city.

text.p: Zaire's crisis entered a critical stage with rebels closing in on the chief economic city while the capital slid further into political anarchy.
International efforts to negotiate an end to six months of civil war showed no sign of a breakthrough after a third day of talks between warring parties in South Africa.
Mortar fire exploded on Monday night on the southern approaches to the second city of Lubumbashi, which has been declared the next main target by rebels, witnesses said.
Explosions first erupted around 8.45 p.m (1845 GMT) and continued into the night, interspersed with the rattle of multi-barrelled rocket launchers.
"It sounds to me like incoming 120 mm mortar fire landing about seven km (four miles) south of the city," a military expert in Lubumbashi said.
Rebels trying to end the 32-year rule of President Mobutu Sese Seko have met little resistance since launching their armed campaign from Zaire's eastern borderlands six months ago.
The heavy gunfire suggested staunchly loyal elements of Mobutu's collapsing army of ill-paid and demoralised troops had decided to put up a last stand in Lubumbashi.
The military expert said earlier he suspected the rebels were trying to lure all the defending troops out to one side of the city, then attack from the other.
The city is the capital of Zaire's lifeline copper and cobalt mining industry that has underpinned Mobutu's hold on the vast central African country.
Earlier in the day a Zaire government army commander said the rebels were about 15 km (10 miles) from the city.
In Kinshasa defence ministry sources said Zaire's Special Presidential Service forces (DSP) had been sent to push back rebels from Kipushi, 30 km (20 miles) southwest of Lubumbashi.
It was not clear if the firing had anything to do with their reported intervention.
Earlier in the day fear gripped Lubumbashi amid reports that rebels had taken Kipushi, which is on the Zambian border.
The fall of Kipushi could not be directly confirmed, but business people in Lubumbashi said the news had come directly from Kipushi residents contacted by telephone.
In South Africa the first talks between envoys from Kinshasa and those of rebel leader Laurent Kabila met through Monday with no tangible sign of any progress in the search for peace.

"What's been happening is the Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and other (South African) representatives spent all day conferring with the leadership of both parties, separately and jointly," a South African spokesman told Reuters.
The spokesman declined to say what progress had been made or when the participants might be ready to make a statement.

In the capital Kinshasa supporters of Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi defied armoured vehicles and tear gas to prevent a parliamentary debate of no-confidence in the controversial politician who took office only last week.

The protesters failed to enter the assembly building but dispersed leaving it surrounded by gendarmes, some of whom openly supported Tshisekedi. The building was under the control of hundreds of troops but with no parliamentarians inside.
Tshisekedi, Mobutu's chief political rival, was appointed last week but parliament has initiated moves to remove him because of his unilateral decision to dissolve the assembly.
Tshisekedi supporters plan more protests for Tuesday.
